question: Developing AI is one of the EU’s top priorities. At the same time, the number of data centres is growing, and significant amounts of electricity and new investments in energy grids are required to keep them running. In some Member States, grid operators are already warning of increasing problems with connecting new capacity. 1.

Does the Commission believe that Europe currently has sufficient energy and modern grids at its disposal to fulfil its AI ambitions, and that the development of AI will not drive up electricity prices for industry and households?

Does the Commission see a real risk that delays in the development of energy infrastructure will hinder the European AI sector and further increase the Union’s dependence on technologies and services from third countries?

What specific measures does the Commission intend to take to ensure that data centres do not consume energy while depriving the rest of European industry and households of access to energy at competitive prices?
answer: The Commission acknowledges that data centres demand is expected to significantly grow in line with the ambition to triple their computing capacity in the next five to seven years to ensure EU technological sovereignty (1). The Cloud and Artificial Intelligence (AI) Development Act (2) proposed measures to accelerate deployment of sustainable cloud and data centre infrastructure.

To contribute to sustainable data centres grid integration, the European Grids package (3) proposed cross-sectorial network planning with involvement of stakeholders, accelerated permit-granting procedures and priority emphasis on grid efficiency in planning.

Under the Strategic Roadmap for Digitalisation and AI in the Energy Sector (4), as well as under AI Factories and the AI Gigafactories initiative (5), the Commission is working with energy and digital industries to develop a model tripartite agreement for the sustainable integration of data centres (6).

The proposal to future-proof electricity bills (7) aims at bringing down electricity costs by designing network charges that incentivise a flexible, system-friendly use of the grid and integration of generation and loads, as well as by ensuring smart and efficient electricity grids and efficient network access.

The Commission is also working on a Data Centre Energy Efficiency Package (8) to introduce a rating scheme (9) for the energy efficiency of data centres. The Commission will also launch a public consultation for possible minimum performance standards for data centres.
